Fall Armyworm.what: A caterpillar (moth larva) that eats maize and sorghum leaves from the inside of the whorl.
Fall Armyworm.signs: Window-pane scraping and ragged holes on young leaves, sawdust-like droppings in the whorl, caterpillars with an upside-down Y on the head.
fix: Check 20 plants in a W pattern; act if 1 in 10 shows fresh damage.
Crush egg masses and small caterpillars by hand.
If damage is above that level, spray a PCPB-registered product (e.g. a Bt product) into the whorl early in the morning, with gloves and mask.
Do not spray if rain is expected within 6 hours.
Fall Armyworm.prevent: Plant early with the rains, rotate with beans, and keep a border of Brachiaria grass with Desmodium (push-pull).

Late Blight.what: A fast-spreading disease of potato and tomato that thrives in cool, wet weather.
Late Blight.signs: Dark, water-soaked patches with pale edges on leaves, white mould underneath in the morning, brown marks on stems.
fix: Remove and bury or burn infected leaves and plants the same day.
Spray a registered protective fungicide (e.g. one containing mancozeb) before rain, following the label.
Water at the base, never on the leaves.
Late Blight.prevent: Use certified seed, space plants for air flow, and keep potato and tomato off the same plot for 3 seasons.

Aphids.what: Small soft insects (green or black) that suck sap from beans, kale and cabbage.
Aphids.signs: Clusters of tiny insects on stems and under leaves, curled leaves, sticky honeydew, black sooty mould, ants on the plant.
fix: Wash them off with a strong spray of water.
Spray soap solution or neem on stems and under leaves; repeat after 5 days.
Only if they keep spreading, use a registered aphicide, following the label.
Aphids.prevent: Check plants weekly and protect ladybirds and other natural enemies.

Bean fly.what: A small fly whose maggots tunnel into young bean stems.
Bean fly.signs: Seedlings wilting and dying, swollen or cracked stem at soil level, tiny holes on leaves.
fix: Earth up soil around the stems so new roots can form above the damage.
Remove and destroy dead seedlings.
Top-dress lightly so surviving plants recover.
Bean fly.prevent: Plant at the start of the rains and use treated seed next season.

Maize Lethal Necrosis.what: A virus disease of maize spread by insects and infected seed.
Maize Lethal Necrosis.signs: Yellow streaks from the leaf edges, leaves drying from the margins, a dead central shoot, poorly filled cobs.
fix: Pull out and destroy infected plants early.
Do not save seed from this crop.
Maize Lethal Necrosis.prevent: Use certified tolerant varieties and plant beans or potato for one season to break the cycle.

Tomato leaf miner (Tuta).what: A small moth whose caterpillars tunnel inside tomato leaves and fruit.
Tomato leaf miner (Tuta).signs: Pale blotches (mines) in leaves, holes in fruit, droppings.
fix: Remove and destroy leaves with mines.
Hang pheromone traps.
Use a registered product only if damage spreads.
Tomato leaf miner (Tuta).prevent: Use insect-proof net in greenhouses and destroy old crop residue.

Striga (witchweed).what: A parasitic weed that attaches to maize and sorghum roots and steals their water and food.
Striga (witchweed).signs: Small plants with bright pink-purple flowers among stunted, yellowing maize.
fix: Pull it out by hand before it flowers, and burn or bury it.
Do not let it set seed (one plant makes thousands of seeds).
Striga (witchweed).prevent: Use push-pull with Desmodium, a Striga-tolerant maize variety, and rotate with beans or groundnut.

Couch grass.what: A creeping grass weed that spreads by underground runners and competes with crops.
Couch grass.signs: Grass spreading through the plot with white runners under the soil.
fix: Dig out the runners completely and dry them in the sun off the plot.
Weed again 2 weeks later to catch regrowth.
Couch grass.prevent: Plough deep in the dry season and keep the ground covered with crop or mulch.

Black-jack (Bidens).what: A fast-growing broad-leaf weed whose spiky seeds stick to clothes.
Black-jack (Bidens).signs: Yellow flowers and needle-like seeds in clusters.
fix: Pull or hoe it out before it flowers.
Weed at weeks 2-3 and 5-6 after the crop comes up.
Black-jack (Bidens).prevent: Weed early and keep it from setting seed.

Wild / prickly lettuce.what: A common broad-leaf weed with toothed, prickly leaves and milky sap.
Wild / prickly lettuce.signs: Upright plant with lobed, toothed leaves, prickles along the leaf midrib, milky sap when cut.
fix: Pull it out with the root before it flowers, wearing gloves.
Remove it from the plot so seeds do not spread.
Wild / prickly lettuce.prevent: Weed early and keep the ground covered.

Weed (species unclear).what: A weed: an unwanted plant that competes with your crop for water, nutrients and light.
Weed (species unclear).signs: A plant you did not sow growing among or around the crop.
fix: Pull it out with the root before it flowers and remove it from the plot.
Keep the crop weed-free for its first 6 weeks.
Weed (species unclear).prevent: Weed early and often; mulch to keep weeds down.

Nutrient deficiency (not a pest).what: The plant is short of a nutrient; no pest or disease is involved.
Nutrient deficiency (not a pest).signs: Pale or yellow leaves across the whole plant, purple tints, stunted growth.
fix: Top-dress with a nitrogen fertiliser (e.g. CAN) for pale maize, or add well-rotted manure.
Ask your officer about a soil test.
Nutrient deficiency (not a pest).prevent: Use manure or compost each season and test the soil every 2-3 seasons.
